planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container trees in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Calimyrna is the American-grown form of the Turkish Smyrna fig and, unlike common-type figs such as Celeste or Brown Turkey, it is a true Smyrna type that will not set a crop without caprification — pollination by the fig wasp Blastophaga psenes carrying pollen from an inedible caprifig planted nearby.

directions: Calimyrna is the California-grown descendant of the ancient Lob Injir fig of Smyrna (modern Izmir), Turkey, brought into the San Joaquin Valley in the late 1800s and still the backbone of California's dried-fig and fig-paste industry. Its large, golden-green fruit ripens to a distinctive nutty, honeyed flavor with a thin skin and an interior packed with edible, crunchy seeds, considered by many growers to have the richest flavor of any commercial fig. Unlike common figs, Calimyrna requires true caprification: a caprifig tree carrying the fig wasp Blastophaga psenes must be planted nearby, or the flowers drop unfertilized and the crop fails, which makes home cultivation far more demanding than self-fertile common-type figs and largely limits it to hot, arid growing regions where the wasp's short breeding window lines up with bloom. In humid Gulf South climates the wasp is absent and caprification is impractical, so Calimyrna is a poor choice outside California's Central Valley and similar dry-summer regions. Where it can be grown, it wants the same deep, well-drained soil, full sun, and minimal winter pruning as other figs, with irrigation timed to avoid splitting as the main crop ripens in late summer.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Fig Production in California
California Rare Fruit Growers — Fig Fact Sheet
USDA Agricultural Research Service — Fig Germplasm and Caprification Research

common_name: Chubby Cheeks Intermediate Bearded Iris (Historic Warburton Pink IB)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes shallowly, top surface exposed to the sun, in late summer to early fall in well-drained soil; Chubby Cheeks is an Intermediate Bearded (IB) iris, blooming shorter and earlier than tall bearded cultivars and dividing more readily as clumps thicken.

directions: Chubby Cheeks is a historically important Intermediate Bearded iris hybridized by Bee Warburton, valued for its ruffled, clear pink self flowers set off by a bright tangerine-orange beard on compact, well-branched stalks blooming ahead of most tall bearded cultivars. Its combination of strong pink pigment, vigorous increase, and dependable garden performance made it a widely grown garden favorite in its era and an important parent behind later pink-toned Median iris breeding, including modern award winners bred generations later. Set rhizomes horizontally with the top exposed to the sun, never buried, since standing moisture causes rot far more readily than this iris is troubled by drought. Divide congested clumps every two to three years after bloom, a bit more often than tall bearded types, since Intermediate Beardeds multiply quickly and become crowded.
sources: American Iris Society — Iris Encyclopedia (wiki.irises.org)
Historic Iris Preservation Society
Schreiner's Gardens — Bearded Iris Culture Guide

common_name: Flame Tokay Grape (Historic Lodi Red Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Flame Tokay is a late-season variety that needs a long, warm growing season to fully color its large berries before fall.

directions: Flame Tokay, usually sold simply as Tokay, is the historic red-skinned table grape that made Lodi, California the self-proclaimed 'Tokay Capital of the World' for much of the twentieth century, complete with an annual Tokay harvest festival once the region's signature civic event. The large, oval, crimson-pink berries form loose, well-filled clusters with crisp, mild, sweet flesh and substantial seeds, eaten fresh off the vine and once shipped nationwide as a fall specialty grape before seedless varieties reshaped the table-grape market. Vines are vigorous and productive but need a long, hot growing season to fully color the thick-skinned berries, and the loose cluster habit helps reduce bunch rot in years with late-season moisture compared with tighter-clustered varieties. Train to a permanent cordon system and prune hard each winter, thinning crowded clusters in early summer to improve berry size, and harvest by taste rather than color alone since Tokay can look ripe before its sugar fully develops.
sources: University of California Cooperative Extension — Lodi Winegrape and Table Grape History
UC Davis Department of Viticulture and Enology — Vitis vinifera Cultivar Database
California Rare Fruit Growers — Grape Fact Sheet

common_name: Ribier Grape (Historic Large Black Seeded Table Grape)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a sturdy trellis in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Ribier is a vigorous, late-ripening variety that benefits from a long, warm season and careful cluster thinning to size its large berries well.

directions: Ribier, grown in Europe under the name Alphonse Lavallée, is a historic French black table grape once a mainstay of the California fresh-market grape trade before seedless varieties largely displaced seeded types in supermarkets. Its very large, round, thick-skinned, jet-black berries have mild, sweet, unassuming flavor rather than intense complexity, but their impressive size and striking color made them a favorite for fruit bowls and holiday displays for much of the twentieth century. Vines are vigorous and productive, ripening late in the season, and the thick skin gives the berries useful resistance to cracking and rot compared with thinner-skinned varieties. Train to a permanent cordon system, prune hard each winter, and thin developing clusters to a manageable number of berries, since Ribier tends to overset and undersized fruit loses the variety's main visual appeal.
sources: UC Davis Department of Viticulture and Enology — Vitis vinifera Cultivar Database
University of California Cooperative Extension — California Table Grape History
California Table Grape Commission — Historic Varieties

common_name: Roger's Red Grape (Ornamental Fall-Color California Grape)

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container vines in spring against a sturdy arbor, fence, or pergola in full sun; Roger's Red is grown chiefly as a deciduous ornamental for its brilliant scarlet fall foliage rather than for its small, tart fruit.

directions: Roger's Red is a fast-growing deciduous ornamental grape discovered by horticulturist Roger Raiche near an old homestead in Northern California and named for him, prized above all for its dramatic autumn color, when the broad leaves turn a saturated scarlet-crimson well before most other fall foliage plants. Although long sold as a straight selection of the native California wild grape, later genetic testing found Roger's Red actually carries wine-grape ancestry alongside its Vitis californica parentage, which likely explains its unusually intense red fall color compared with the species. It bears small, tart, blue-black grapes in loose clusters that are edible but grown mainly for wildlife value rather than fresh eating, since the true ornamental draw is the vine's vigorous habit and spectacular foliage display. Train it onto a strong arbor, fence, or pergola where its twining habit and fall color can be appreciated, and prune hard each winter to keep its vigorous growth in bounds; established vines are drought-tolerant and need little summer irrigation.
sources: Calscape (California Native Plant Society) — Vitis californica 'Roger's Red'
UC Davis Department of Viticulture and Enology — Native California Grape Genetics

common_name: Ugni Blanc Grape (Trebbiano, Cognac and Armagnac Distilling Grape)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Ugni Blanc buds and ripens late, so it needs a long growing season but is correspondingly less prone to spring frost damage than early-budding varieties.

directions: Ugni Blanc, known in Italy as Trebbiano Toscano and historically as Saint-Emilion in the Cognac region, is among the most widely planted white grapes on earth, prized less for varietal wine than for producing the thin, high-acid, neutral-flavored base wine that is distilled into Cognac and Armagnac brandy. Its naturally high acidity, low sugar accumulation, and productivity are exactly the traits distillers want, since a lean, acidic base wine distills cleanly and ages well in oak, while the same neutral character makes it a workhorse blending and everyday table wine grape across Italy and southern France. The vine buds and ripens late in the season, which helps it dodge spring frost but means it needs a long, warm growing season to fully mature its large, productive clusters. It shows good resistance to many fungal diseases relative to thinner-skinned fine wine grapes, though bunch rot can still develop in wet years with dense canopies. Train to a permanent trellis, manage the vigorous canopy for good air movement, and harvest based on acid retention rather than sugar level if the goal is a base wine for distillation.
sources: UC Davis Department of Viticulture and Enology — Vitis vinifera Cultivar Database
Bureau National Interprofessionnel du Cognac — Grape Varieties
Wine Institute — Grape Variety Reference

common_name: Cinsaut Grape (Cinsault, Historic Southern French and South African Red)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container-grown vines in early spring on a trellis system in deep, well-drained soil in full sun; Cinsaut is heat- and drought-tolerant once established and performs well on the same lean, sunny sites favored for other southern French Rhone-style reds.

directions: Cinsaut, also spelled Cinsault and grown in South Africa for generations under the name Hermitage, is a historic red wine grape of southern France's Languedoc and Provence regions, valued for large, loose clusters of thin-skinned berries that produce soft, lightly colored, fruity wine most often used in blends and rosé rather than bottled alone. Its vigor, heat tolerance, and reliable heavy cropping made it one of the most widely planted red grapes in the south of France for much of the twentieth century, prized by growers even as its soft tannins and pale color kept it out of the great varietal reds. Cinsaut carries outsized historical importance as one of the two parent grapes, crossed with Pinot Noir in 1925, of South Africa's signature Pinotage variety. Old, dry-farmed Cinsaut vines are increasingly sought after today for characterful, juicy varietal reds and natural wine blends. Train to a permanent trellis, manage the vigorous canopy for airflow to limit bunch rot in the loosely packed but still humidity-sensitive clusters, and thin crop in wet years to concentrate flavor, since Cinsaut left to overcrop produces thin, diluted wine.
sources: UC Davis Department of Viticulture and Enology — Vitis vinifera Cultivar Database
